content: The carbon cycle describes the movement of carbon atoms between Earth's atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, and lithosphere. Carbon flows between these reservoirs through various biogeochemical processes. Carbon enters the atmosphere primarily as carbon dioxide (COâ) through respiration, combustion, and volcanic activity. Plants remove atmospheric COâ through photosynthesis, converting it to carbohydrates and incorporating it into biomassâthis represents the fastest major carbon transfer mechanism. Through the food web, carbon moves from producers to consumers and decomposers. When organisms die, their carbon returns to the atmosphere through decomposition or becomes buried and compressed, eventually forming fossil fuels over millions of years. The ocean acts as Earth's largest carbon reservoir, absorbing about 25% of atmospheric COâ. Dissolved COâ forms carbonic acid, which can dissociate into bicarbonate and carbonate ions. Marine organisms use carbonate to build shells and skeletons, which can accumulate as limestone after death. Human activities have significantly altered the carbon cycle, primarily through fossil fuel combustion and deforestation, which release carbon that was previously sequestered in long-term geological reservoirs. This has increased atmospheric COâ from approximately 280 ppm in pre-industrial times to over 410 ppm today, enhancing the greenhouse effect and contributing to climate change.

scenario.title: Carbon Journey Simulator
scenario.content: Students track carbon atoms through a school-themed representation of the global carbon cycle, where classrooms, cafeteria, garden, parking lot, and recycling center represent different carbon reservoirs and processes. The simulation visualizes carbon movement between these spaces, showing transformations between different molecular forms. Students can manipulate factors affecting carbon flows, such as photosynthesis rates, fossil fuel use, ocean temperature, and land use changes. The system provides real-time data on carbon distribution across reservoirs and flux rates between them. Interactive tools allow students to tag and follow individual carbon atoms through complete cycles, create and test interventions to rebalance carbon flows, and compare natural versus human-influenced cycle dynamics. Challenge scenarios require students to design carbon management strategies that balance environmental, economic, and social factors.

hypothesis.description: Students will trace carbon pathways through Earth's systems by analyzing flux rates and residence times in different reservoirs. They will predict how natural processes and human activities affect carbon distribution, and explain the connections between the carbon cycle and climate regulation.
